signals.headline: Zero borrowing; balance-sheet identity closes cleanly on internal borrowing across all five printed years
signals.why_it_matters: Verified quiet on the borrowing side. Zero-to-zero tie against our PWLB file. The whole £30.9m financing requirement is met from cash — a stance the paper is explicit about, and one that becomes tighter as reserves halve from £97.4m to £55.2m over the strategy window.

signals.why_it_matters: App B §2 balance-sheet table. Reserves depletion is deliberate and disclosed — Executive Summary uses 'much weakened financial position as it hands over to a successor body'. Investment income prudential indicator falls 29% → 19% of net revenue stream over the same window (§4.18).

signals.headline: £56m commercial property (7.3% net return); £0.5m equity + £4m potential loan facility to housing company
signals.why_it_matters: App C §11, §3, §6. Property portfolio produces £4.1m net income against a total revenue stream in which commercial + service investment income was 29% in 2024/25. Swan Walk retail equity written down £8.4m against £9.5m purchase (App C §13, disclosed transparently); recent retail written down £6.5m against £14.7m; legacy light industrial has done the offsetting work (+£9.4m). Portfolio limit £70m; WAULT 14yr; five tenants over 5% of net property income.

courses_named: Investing surplus cash: pooled funds and strategic allocation
officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Capital Strategy that went to Audit Committee on 26 November, ahead of it going forward to Cabinet in January and Council in February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The strategy is unusually clean and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

On the reconciliation, there isn't one to run in the usual sense. Appendix B paragraph 1 says the Council held no borrowing on 30 September, paragraph 4.3 confirms it, and paragraph 7.1 says there is no debt interest budget because none is envisaged. Our PWLB file returns nothing against Horsham District Council either. So it's a zero-to-zero tie rather than a match on a positive figure — worth stating once, because we don't want to imply anything you hold is uncounted.

What is unusual across the councils we've read is the shape of the position sitting behind that zero. Your CFR is £36.8m at 31 March 2025, of which £5.9m is IFRS 16 lease liability and the rest — £30.9m — is internal borrowing done from cash. The balance-sheet identity (CFR minus external minus other long-term liabilities equals internal borrowing) closes on every one of the five printed years in Appendix B's paragraph 2 table without any adjustment. That is rare. Most books we read need a note to reconcile.

The part that stood out is the trajectory. Useable reserves fall from £97.4m to £55.2m and investments from £70m to £31.5m across the four years of Appendix B's balance-sheet table. Long-term investments collapse from £35m to £2m in the final year alone, with short-term jumping from £1m to £30m as strategic pooled funds and long bonds are brought back to cash — that's a real disposal window inside the strategy period, and the timing of it is a decision that matters. On the paper's own indicator (paragraph 4.18) commercial and service investment net income runs from 29% of your net revenue stream today to 19% by 2028/29, which is the size of the compression the reorganisation runway is asking the general fund to absorb. Paragraph 7.1's £3.0m treasury income forecast at 4.1% on £74m is testable against the mid-year composition your Appendix B sets out — £85.7m at a blended 4.4% at 30 September, dropping as new money invests at Bank Rate per paragraph 2.2. Bank Rate is 3.75% today, which is exactly where Arlingclose's central case in Appendix A puts it, so the assumption is on track for now. The forward curve tells you when it changes — we publish the implied Bank Rate path from SONIA daily rather than quarterly, at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

And one thing from the commercial book, offered because it is in your paper and because the composition is interesting. The £56m portfolio contains a £8.4m loss on Swan Walk against £9.5m purchase and £6.5m on recent retail against £14.7m purchase, both fully offset in the totals by the £9.4m gain on legacy light industrial against a £9.3m cost. The industrial position is doing a lot of work in a portfolio that reports a small net gain. Your Appendix C paragraph 20 requires £5m of the portfolio to be saleable as a going concern within six months, which is a real constraint against a rate environment that has moved against yields on the asset class since some of those recent purchases were made. Not a recommendation — we don't sell treasury products and we don't advise. Just the shape of the number.

On training, three fit given where your paper sits. Cash-flow forecasting & daily cash, because your strategy runs on cash management rather than debt management. Devolution & reorganisation: the treasury view, because the successor-authority framing runs through the whole strategy. And Investing surplus cash: pooled funds and strategic allocation, because of the composition question that the 2028/29 step-down in long-term investments raises. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

July's sector borrowing was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. Your paper is explicit that borrowing is not planned and that the sources approved in Appendix B paragraph 5 are there as an option only. The monthly draw data is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — worth knowing what the sector is doing in case the successor authority conversation ever turns that way. On the wider CIPFA angle, the forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates are putting the liability benchmark in front of everyone. Your paragraph 4.5 explicitly runs a zero benchmark because external borrowing is zero — worth knowing the shape of the interactive comparator we've built for the councils that run the more usual frame.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
